nodes.label: Electron shell arrangement and outer shell electrons
nodes.objective: Recall that atoms have electrons arranged in shells and that the outer shell electrons determine bonding behaviour.
essentialPoints: Electrons occupy shells around the nucleus
The outer (highest) shell electrons are involved in bonding
Group number relates to number of outer shell electrons

nodes.label: Three types of strong chemical bond: ionic, covalent, metallic
nodes.objective: State the three types of strong chemical bonding and the particles/forces involved in each.
essentialPoints: Ionic bonding: electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions
Covalent bonding: atoms sharing pairs of electrons
Metallic bonding: atoms sharing delocalised electrons
Bonding explained via electrostatic forces and electron transfer/sharing

nodes.label: Which substances show which bond type (metal+nonmetal, nonmetal elements/compounds, metals/alloys)
nodes.objective: Identify which type of bonding occurs in a given substance based on its composition.
essentialPoints: Ionic bonding occurs in compounds of metals with non-metals
Covalent bonding occurs in non-metallic elements and compounds of non-metals
Metallic bonding occurs in metallic elements and alloys

nodes.label: Formation of ions by electron transfer (metal loses, non-metal gains)
nodes.objective: Explain how metal and non-metal atoms form ions by losing or gaining electrons.
essentialPoints: Metal atoms lose outer shell electrons to become positive ions
Non-metal atoms gain electrons to become negative ions
This occurs when a metal atom reacts with a non-metal atom

nodes.label: Ions formed by Groups 1,2,6,7 gain noble gas electronic structure
nodes.objective: State that ions formed from Groups 1, 2, 6 and 7 have the electronic structure of a noble gas.
essentialPoints: Group 1/2 metals lose electrons to reach noble gas structure
Group 6/7 non-metals gain electrons to reach noble gas structure

nodes.label: Working out ion charge from group number (Groups 1,2,6,7)
nodes.objective: Deduce the charge on an ion of a Group 1, 2, 6 or 7 element from its group number.
essentialPoints: Group 1 ions are 1+, Group 2 ions are 2+
Group 6 ions are 2-, Group 7 ions are 1-

nodes.label: Drawing dot and cross diagrams for ionic compounds
nodes.objective: Draw dot and cross diagrams showing electron transfer for ionic compounds formed from Group 1/2 metals with Group 6/7 non-metals.
essentialPoints: Diagram shows electron transfer from metal to non-metal
Ions shown with square brackets and charges
Only outer shell electrons are shown

nodes.label: Ionic compound as a giant lattice held by electrostatic forces (ionic bonding)
nodes.objective: Define an ionic compound as a giant structure of ions held together by strong electrostatic forces acting in all directions.
essentialPoints: Giant structure of oppositely charged ions
Strong electrostatic forces of attraction act in all directions in the lattice
This is called ionic bonding

nodes.label: Structure of sodium chloride (dot-and-cross, ball-and-stick, 2D/3D representations)
nodes.objective: Recognise sodium chloride's structure represented in different diagram forms.
essentialPoints: NaCl represented via dot-and-cross, ball-and-stick, 2D and 3D lattice diagrams
Only NaCl structure required in detail

nodes.label: Deducing a compound is ionic from a structural diagram
nodes.objective: Identify that a given structure diagram represents an ionic compound.
essentialPoints: Recognise repeating lattice pattern of alternating ions as ionic

nodes.label: Limitations of dot-and-cross/ball-and-stick/2D/3D models for giant ionic structures
nodes.objective: Describe the limitations of different representations of giant ionic lattices.
essentialPoints: Ball-and-stick implies fixed bonds/gaps not present in reality
2D diagrams cannot show the full 3D extent of the lattice
No single model shows relative sizes, scale or that forces act in all directions

nodes.label: Working out empirical formula of an ionic compound from a model/diagram
nodes.objective: Determine the empirical formula of an ionic compound by counting ions shown in a model or diagram.
essentialPoints: Count ratio of each type of ion shown in the diagram
Express as simplest whole-number ratio (empirical formula)

nodes.label: Covalent bonding: atoms sharing pairs of electrons
nodes.objective: Define covalent bonding as atoms sharing pairs of electrons, forming strong bonds.
essentialPoints: Atoms share pairs of electrons
Covalent bonds between atoms are strong

nodes.label: Recognising common small molecules from chemical formula
nodes.objective: Recognise common substances that consist of small molecules from their chemical formula.
essentialPoints: Small molecule substances have simple molecular formulae (e.g. H2O, CO2)

nodes.label: Drawing dot and cross diagrams for named covalent molecules
nodes.objective: Draw dot and cross diagrams for hydrogen, chlorine, oxygen, nitrogen, hydrogen chloride, water, ammonia and methane.
essentialPoints: Show shared electron pairs between bonded atoms
Show all outer shell electrons for each atom including lone pairs
Covers H2, Cl2, O2, N2, HCl, H2O, NH3, CH4

nodes.label: Representing covalent bonds using lines (single bonds) in molecules, polymers and giant structures
nodes.objective: Represent covalent bonds using a line to show a single bond in small molecules, polymer repeating units and giant covalent structures.
essentialPoints: A line represents one shared pair of electrons (single covalent bond)
Used for small molecules, polymer repeat units and giant structures

nodes.label: Representing polymers with repeating unit notation (n)
nodes.objective: Represent polymer structures using a repeating unit in brackets with subscript n.
essentialPoints: Polymers shown as a repeat unit in brackets with n outside
n represents a large number of repeat units

nodes.label: Recognising substances as small molecules, polymers or giant covalent structures from bonding diagrams
nodes.objective: Classify a substance as a small molecule, polymer or giant covalent structure from a diagram of its bonding.
essentialPoints: Small molecules show a fixed small number of atoms bonded together
Polymers show a repeating unit with n
Giant covalent structures show an extended repeating network

nodes.label: Limitations of dot-and-cross/ball-and-stick/2D/3D models for molecules and giant covalent structures
nodes.objective: Describe the limitations of different representations of covalent molecules and giant structures.
essentialPoints: Ball-and-stick models exaggerate bond lengths/gaps between atoms
2D diagrams cannot show true 3D shape or bond angles
Models do not show relative sizes of atoms accurately

nodes.label: Deducing molecular formula from a model or diagram of a molecule
nodes.objective: Deduce the molecular formula of a substance from a model or diagram showing its atoms and bonds.
essentialPoints: Count the number of each type of atom shown in the diagram/model

nodes.label: Metallic bonding: giant structure with delocalised outer shell electrons
nodes.objective: Define metallic bonding as the sharing of delocalised outer shell electrons in a giant structure of metal atoms.
essentialPoints: Metals are giant structures of atoms in a regular pattern
Outer shell electrons become delocalised and free to move through the structure
Sharing of delocalised electrons gives strong metallic bonds

nodes.label: Recognising metallic giant structures from bonding diagrams
nodes.objective: Recognise a metallic giant structure from a diagram showing positive ions in a sea of delocalised electrons.
essentialPoints: Diagram shows regular array of positive ions surrounded by delocalised electrons

nodes.label: Simple particle model of solid, liquid and gas states
nodes.objective: Describe the three states of matter using the simple particle model (particles as solid spheres).
essentialPoints: Three states: solid, liquid, gas
Particles represented as small solid spheres
Arrangement/movement of spheres differs between states

nodes.label: Naming changes of state: melting, freezing, boiling, condensing at melting/boiling point
nodes.objective: Name the changes of state and state that they occur at the melting point or boiling point.
essentialPoints: Melting and freezing occur at the melting point
Boiling and condensing occur at the boiling point

nodes.label: Energy needed for state change depends on strength of forces between particles (bonding/structure)
nodes.objective: Explain that the energy required to change state depends on the strength of the forces between particles, which depends on bonding type and structure.
essentialPoints: Stronger forces between particles require more energy to change state
Nature of particles/forces depends on the type of bonding and structure
Stronger forces mean higher melting and boiling points

nodes.label: Predicting the state of a substance at a given temperature from melting/boiling point data
nodes.objective: Predict whether a substance is solid, liquid or gas at a given temperature using its melting and boiling points.
essentialPoints: Compare given temperature to melting point and boiling point
Below melting point = solid, between = liquid, above boiling point = gas

nodes.label: Atoms themselves do not have the bulk properties of the material
nodes.objective: Recognise that individual atoms do not display the bulk (macroscopic) properties of the material they form.
essentialPoints: A single atom cannot be described as having melting point, hardness etc.
Bulk properties arise from the collective structure and bonding of many atoms

nodes.label: (HT) Limitations of the simple particle model (no forces, spheres, solid inelastic)
nodes.objective: Explain the limitations of the simple particle model in representing changes of state, given that it shows no forces and solid inelastic spheres.
essentialPoints: Model has no forces between particles, unlike reality
Particles shown as solid spheres, not representing internal structure
Spheres are shown as inelastic, unlike real atoms/molecules

nodes.label: State symbols (s), (l), (g), (aq) in chemical equations
nodes.objective: Use the correct state symbols in chemical equations to represent solids, liquids, gases and aqueous solutions.
essentialPoints: (s) = solid, (l) = liquid, (g) = gas, (aq) = aqueous solution

nodes.label: Ionic compounds have high melting and boiling points
nodes.objective: Explain why ionic compounds have high melting and boiling points in terms of the strength and number of ionic bonds.
essentialPoints: Giant ionic lattice has strong electrostatic forces in all directions
Large amounts of energy needed to break many strong bonds

nodes.label: Ionic compounds conduct electricity when molten or dissolved (free ions), not when solid
nodes.objective: Explain why ionic compounds conduct electricity when molten or in aqueous solution but not as solids.
essentialPoints: Ions are free to move when molten or dissolved, allowing charge to flow
In solid state ions are held in fixed positions in the lattice and cannot move

nodes.label: Weak intermolecular forces between small molecules vs strong covalent bonds within them
nodes.objective: Explain that small molecular substances have weak intermolecular forces between molecules, distinct from the strong covalent bonds within molecules.
essentialPoints: Intermolecular forces act between separate molecules, not within them
These forces are much weaker than covalent bonds
When melting/boiling, intermolecular forces are overcome, not covalent bonds

nodes.label: Small molecular substances have low melting/boiling points due to weak intermolecular forces
nodes.objective: Explain why substances made of small molecules are usually gases or liquids with low melting and boiling points.
essentialPoints: Only weak intermolecular forces need to be overcome to melt/boil
Little energy is needed, giving low melting and boiling points

nodes.label: Intermolecular forces (and mp/bp) increase with molecule size
nodes.objective: Explain the trend that larger molecules have stronger intermolecular forces and therefore higher melting and boiling points.
essentialPoints: Intermolecular forces increase in strength as molecule size increases
Larger molecules therefore have higher melting and boiling points

nodes.label: Small molecular substances do not conduct electricity (no overall charge)
nodes.objective: Explain why substances made of small molecules do not conduct electricity.
essentialPoints: Molecules have no overall electric charge
No free ions or delocalised electrons to carry charge

nodes.label: Polymers are solids at room temperature due to strong covalent bonds and relatively strong intermolecular forces
nodes.objective: Explain why polymers are solid at room temperature, referencing bonding within and between polymer chains.
essentialPoints: Atoms within polymer molecules linked by strong covalent bonds
Intermolecular forces between long polymer chains are relatively strong (compared to small molecules)
Combined effect makes polymers solid at room temperature

nodes.label: Recognising polymers from diagrams of bonding and structure
nodes.objective: Recognise a polymer from a diagram showing its repeating unit and bonding.
essentialPoints: Identify repeating unit notation and long chain structure as a polymer

nodes.label: Giant covalent structures are solids with very high melting points
nodes.objective: Explain that giant covalent structures have very high melting points because strong covalent bonds throughout the structure must be overcome.
essentialPoints: All atoms linked by strong covalent bonds throughout the structure
These bonds must be broken (not just weak intermolecular forces) to melt/boil
Examples: diamond, graphite, silicon dioxide

nodes.label: Recognising giant covalent structures from diagrams of bonding and structure
nodes.objective: Recognise a giant covalent structure from a diagram showing an extended network of covalently bonded atoms.
essentialPoints: Identify a repeating extended network with no separate molecules as giant covalent

nodes.label: Metals have high melting and boiling points due to strong metallic bonding
nodes.objective: Explain that most metals have high melting and boiling points due to strong metallic bonds throughout the giant structure.
essentialPoints: Metals are giant structures held by strong metallic bonding
Large amounts of energy needed to break many strong metallic bonds

nodes.label: Metal atoms arranged in layers, allowing bending and shaping (malleability/ductility)
nodes.objective: Explain that pure metals can be bent and shaped because their atoms are arranged in layers that can slide over each other.
essentialPoints: Atoms in pure metals arranged in ordered layers
Layers of atoms can slide over one another, allowing bending/shaping

nodes.label: Alloys are harder than pure metals (distortion of atomic layers)
nodes.objective: Explain why alloys are harder than pure metals in terms of distortion of the layers of atoms.
essentialPoints: Pure metals are too soft for many uses so are mixed with other metals to form alloys
Different sized atoms in an alloy distort the regular layers
Distorted layers cannot slide over each other as easily, making alloys harder

nodes.label: Metals conduct electricity via delocalised electrons carrying charge
nodes.objective: Explain why metals are good conductors of electricity in terms of delocalised electrons carrying charge.
essentialPoints: Delocalised electrons are free to move through the metal structure
These moving electrons carry electrical charge through the metal

nodes.label: Metals conduct thermal energy via delocalised electrons transferring energy
nodes.objective: Explain why metals are good conductors of thermal energy in terms of delocalised electrons transferring energy.
essentialPoints: Delocalised electrons transfer thermal energy through the metal structure

nodes.label: Diamond structure: each carbon forms 4 covalent bonds in a giant covalent lattice
nodes.objective: Describe the structure of diamond as each carbon atom forming four covalent bonds with other carbon atoms in a giant lattice.
essentialPoints: Each carbon atom forms four covalent bonds to other carbon atoms
Forms a rigid giant covalent structure

nodes.label: Explaining diamond's properties (very hard, very high mp, non-conductor) from its structure
nodes.objective: Explain the properties of diamond (hardness, high melting point, non-conductivity) in terms of its structure and bonding.
essentialPoints: Very hard because many strong covalent bonds resist deformation in all directions
Very high melting point because many strong covalent bonds must be broken
Does not conduct electricity because there are no free electrons or ions

nodes.label: Graphite structure: each carbon forms 3 covalent bonds in hexagonal layers, one delocalised electron per atom
nodes.objective: Describe the structure of graphite as layers of hexagonal rings with three covalent bonds per carbon atom and one delocalised electron per atom, with no bonds between layers.
essentialPoints: Each carbon atom forms three covalent bonds with three other carbon atoms
Forms layers of hexagonal rings
No covalent bonds exist between the layers
One electron per carbon atom is delocalised

nodes.label: Explaining graphite's properties (soft/slippery, conducts electricity, high mp) from its structure
nodes.objective: Explain the properties of graphite (softness, electrical conductivity, high melting point) in terms of its layered structure and delocalised electrons.
essentialPoints: Layers can slide over each other as there are no covalent bonds between layers, making graphite soft/slippery
Delocalised electrons allow graphite to conduct electricity, similar to metals
High melting point because strong covalent bonds within layers must be broken

nodes.label: Graphene as a single layer of graphite
nodes.objective: Describe graphene as a single layer of graphite, one atom thick.
essentialPoints: Graphene is a single layer of carbon atoms arranged in hexagonal rings
It is essentially one layer of graphite

nodes.label: Explaining graphene's properties and uses in electronics and composites
nodes.objective: Explain the properties of graphene in terms of its structure and bonding and relate these to its uses in electronics and composites.
essentialPoints: Delocalised electrons make graphene an excellent electrical conductor
Strong covalent bonds in a single layer make it strong yet very thin/light
These properties make it useful in electronics and composite materials

nodes.label: Fullerenes: hollow carbon molecules based on hexagonal (plus 5/7) rings, e.g. Buckminsterfullerene C60
nodes.objective: Describe fullerenes as hollow-shaped carbon molecules based on hexagonal rings, sometimes including five- or seven-membered rings.
essentialPoints: Fullerenes are molecules of carbon atoms with hollow shapes
Structure based mainly on hexagonal rings, may include rings of five or seven carbons
Buckminsterfullerene (C60) was the first fullerene discovered, with a spherical shape

nodes.label: Carbon nanotubes: cylindrical fullerenes with high length-to-diameter ratio
nodes.objective: Describe carbon nanotubes as cylindrical fullerenes with very high length to diameter ratios and their uses.
essentialPoints: Nanotubes are cylindrical fullerene structures
Very high length to diameter ratio
Useful in nanotechnology, electronics and materials due to strength and conductivity

nodes.label: Recognising graphene and fullerenes from diagrams/descriptions of bonding and structure
nodes.objective: Recognise graphene and fullerenes (including nanotubes) from diagrams or descriptions of their structure.
essentialPoints: Identify single hexagonal sheet as graphene
Identify hollow spherical/cylindrical carbon cage structures as fullerenes/nanotubes

nodes.label: Examples of uses of fullerenes including carbon nanotubes
nodes.objective: Give examples of the uses of fullerenes, including carbon nanotubes.
essentialPoints: Fullerenes used for drug delivery, as catalysts, lubricants
Nanotubes used in electronics, reinforcing composite materials, nanotechnology

nodes.label: Nanoscience size range (1-100 nm) compared to fine (PM2.5) and coarse (PM10) particles
nodes.objective: State the size range of nanoparticles (1-100 nm) and compare this to fine particles (PM2.5) and coarse particles (PM10).
essentialPoints: Nanoparticles are 1-100 nm in size (a few hundred atoms)
Fine particles (PM2.5) have diameters 100-2500 nm
Coarse particles (PM10, dust) have diameters 2.5x10^-6 to 1x10^-5 m

externalPrerequisites.prerequisiteConcept: Standard form and order of magnitude calculations (Topic 0)

nodes.label: Comparing nanoparticle dimensions to typical atom/molecule dimensions
nodes.objective: Compare nanoparticle dimensions to the typical dimensions of atoms and molecules using estimation and order-of-magnitude reasoning.
essentialPoints: Nanoparticles are of the order of a few hundred atoms across
Atoms/molecules are roughly 0.1-0.5 nm, much smaller than a nanoparticle

nodes.label: Surface area to volume ratio increases by factor of 10 as cube side decreases by factor of 10
nodes.objective: Calculate how surface area to volume ratio changes as the size of a cube decreases, showing the ratio increases by a factor of 10 when the side decreases by a factor of 10.
essentialPoints: Surface area to volume ratio = surface area / volume
As cube side length decreases by factor of 10, SA:V ratio increases by factor of 10

externalPrerequisites.prerequisiteConcept: Surface area and volume of cubes (Topic 0 maths skills)

nodes.label: Nanoparticles have different properties from bulk material due to high surface area to volume ratio
nodes.objective: Explain that nanoparticles may have different properties from the same material in bulk because of their high surface area to volume ratio, and that smaller quantities may be needed to be effective.
essentialPoints: High surface area to volume ratio changes reactivity/behaviour compared to bulk
Smaller quantities of nanoparticulate material may be needed to be as effective as bulk material

nodes.label: Applications of nanoparticles (medicine, electronics, cosmetics/sun creams, deodorants, catalysts)
nodes.objective: Recall applications of nanoparticles in medicine, electronics, cosmetics and sun creams, deodorants, and as catalysts.
essentialPoints: Uses include medicine, electronics, cosmetics/sun creams, deodorants, catalysts

nodes.label: Possible risks associated with the use of nanoparticles
nodes.objective: Explain that there are possible risks associated with the use of nanoparticles, such as unknown effects on health and the environment.
essentialPoints: Nanoparticles may be able to enter cells or the bloodstream due to their small size
Long-term health and environmental effects are not yet fully known
High surface area to volume ratio may increase toxicity or reactivity in the body

nodes.label: Evaluating the use of nanoparticles for a specified purpose (benefits vs risks)
nodes.objective: Given appropriate information, evaluate the use of nanoparticles for a specified purpose by weighing benefits against risks.
essentialPoints: Weigh advantages (e.g. effectiveness, small quantities needed, specific applications) against risks (e.g. unknown health/environmental effects)
Judgement should be grounded in given information about the specified purpose
